concepts.name: Agency Dial (0–4)
concepts.definition: A continuous 0–4 scale measuring the degree of autonomous decision-making in a system: 0 = no autonomy (pure pipeline), 1 = single LLM call, 2 = LLM with tools (fixed flow), 3 = LLM chooses tool sequence, 4 = LLM sets own goals and spins up sub-agents. Replaces the binary "is it an agent?" question with an operational, measurable spectrum.
concepts.notes: Central framing concept for the entire course. Enables the decision framework in lesson 1.3 — "what dial setting do I need?"

concepts.name: Agent Definition (Russell-Norvig + Modern LLM)
concepts.definition: An agent is anything that perceives its environment through sensors and acts upon it via actuators (Russell-Norvig). The modern LLM-agent extension adds four properties: (1) LLM as reasoning engine, (2) tool use to affect the world, (3) memory across steps, (4) goal-directed multi-step behavior. The key distinguishing feature vs. a chatbot is persistent action in the world beyond a single response.
concepts.notes: Grounds the course in classical AI theory while bridging to modern LLM practice. Four properties explicitly called out.

concepts.name: Four Properties of an LLM Agent
concepts.definition: The four defining properties that distinguish an LLM agent from a plain chatbot or pipeline: (1) LLM as the core reasoning/planning engine, (2) tool use — ability to call external functions and APIs to affect the world, (3) memory — state that persists beyond a single LLM call, (4) goal-directedness — pursuing multi-step objectives rather than responding to one prompt.
concepts.notes: Acts as the specification checklist for classifying any system on the agency dial.

concepts.name: Cost of Agency
concepts.definition: The set of drawbacks that increase with the agency dial: latency (more steps = more time), cost (more LLM calls = more tokens = higher spend), unpredictability (harder to test, audit, and guarantee behavior), and error compounding (mistakes cascade across multi-step chains). Justifies the heuristic "use the lowest dial setting that solves the problem."
concepts.notes: Directly motivates the decision framework in 1.3. Also connects to Module 9 (cost optimization) and Module 8 (eval).

concepts.name: Symbolic Agents (1956–1990)
concepts.definition: Early AI agents based on explicit symbolic logic, rule engines, and knowledge bases (e.g., STRIPS planner, MYCIN expert system). They encode world knowledge as hand-crafted rules and search over symbol structures. Key limitation: brittleness — they fail outside the narrow domain of their rules, and knowledge engineering is expensive. Key survival: the idea of explicit planning and structured state representation.
concepts.notes: Historical context; explicit planning survives in Plan-and-Solve paradigm (lesson 1.4).

concepts.name: Reinforcement Learning Agents (1990–2017)
concepts.definition: Agents that learn policies by maximizing cumulative reward through interaction with an environment (e.g., TD-Gammon, AlphaGo, Atari DQN). Formally modeled as MDPs. Key contribution: the concepts of state, action, reward, and policy — which persist into modern LLM agent design. Key limitation: require massive interaction data and do not transfer well across domains.
concepts.notes: MDP formalism carried forward into Module 2 (Mathematical Foundations). Provides the vocabulary of state/action/reward used throughout.

concepts.name: LLM Agent Era (2022+)
concepts.definition: The current generation of agents that use large language models as the reasoning engine, inheriting zero-shot/few-shot generalization from pre-training. Key enablers: instruction-following capability, in-context learning, tool-use via function calling (2023+), and long-context windows. LLMs allow agents to be built without reward engineering or domain-specific training, dramatically lowering the cost of agent construction.
concepts.notes: Explains why this course exists now. Key insight: LLMs absorb the "world knowledge" that symbolic agents needed to hard-code.

concepts.name: Ideas That Survived the AI Paradigm Shifts
concepts.definition: Concepts that proved durable across symbolic → RL → LLM agent eras: (1) explicit state representation (now: context window + memory), (2) planning (now: Plan-and-Solve, CoT), (3) tool use / actuation, (4) evaluation against ground truth, (5) the perceive-reason-act loop. Understanding what survived helps practitioners avoid re-inventing solved problems and correctly apply historical lessons.
concepts.notes: The "what survived" framing prevents cargo-culting. Shows intellectual lineage for ReAct, Plan-and-Solve, etc.

concepts.name: Agent vs. Workflow vs. Pipeline Decision Framework
concepts.definition: A five-question framework to determine the right dial setting for a given problem: (1) Is the task decomposable into deterministic steps? → pipeline. (2) Are steps known in advance? → workflow. (3) Does the system need to choose its own tool sequence? → agent (dial 3). (4) Does it need sub-goals and spawned agents? → agent (dial 4). (5) What is the cost of error? — higher cost pushes toward lower dial settings with human oversight. The framework prevents over-engineering.
concepts.notes: The most practically actionable concept in Module 1. Directly addresses the "most common mistake" called out in the module objectives.

concepts.name: Pipeline (Dial 0)
concepts.definition: A data-processing chain with no LLM calls or with LLM calls at fixed, predetermined positions in a static DAG. Inputs flow through a fixed sequence of transformations; no branching or decision-making by an LLM. Highest predictability, lowest cost, easiest to test and audit. Appropriate when all steps are known, deterministic, and the problem is fully specified.
concepts.notes: Baseline against which agents are contrasted. Many "agent" use cases are better served by pipelines.

concepts.name: Workflow (Dial 1–2)
concepts.definition: A process where an LLM is called at one or more steps but the overall control flow is predetermined by the engineer. The LLM may select among a fixed set of branches (dial 2), but it does not dynamically compose tool chains or spawn sub-agents. More testable than full agents; appropriate when the space of decisions is bounded and enumerable.
concepts.notes: The "sweet spot" for many enterprise use cases that don't need full autonomy.

concepts.name: ReAct Paradigm
concepts.definition: Reasoning + Acting interleaved loop: the LLM alternates between (1) Thought — explicit natural-language reasoning about what to do next, (2) Action — emitting a tool call or output, and (3) Observation — receiving the tool result back into context. This loop repeats until a terminal condition. Published by Yao et al. (2022). Core insight: making the reasoning trace explicit improves decision quality and debuggability compared to silent chain-of-thought.
concepts.notes: The most widely-deployed agent paradigm. Foundation for Module 4 (Sherpa v1). Three-component loop (Thought/Action/Observation) is the teachable unit.

concepts.name: Reflexion Paradigm
concepts.definition: An extension of ReAct that adds a self-critique loop: after a trajectory fails (or after each episode), the agent generates verbal self-reflection on what went wrong and stores this reflection in memory for the next attempt. The agent then retries with its own critique as additional context. Shinn et al. (2023). Key advantage over plain ReAct: systematic error correction without gradient updates. Key failure mode: the agent's critique can be wrong or self-serving.
concepts.notes: Extends ReAct with memory-backed self-correction. Used in Module 4 lesson 4.3 (Sherpa self-critique).

concepts.name: Plan-and-Solve Paradigm
concepts.definition: A two-phase agent paradigm: (1) Planning phase — the LLM generates an explicit, structured multi-step plan before taking any actions, (2) Solve phase — the LLM executes each plan step, potentially using ReAct sub-loops per step. Wang et al. (2023). Key advantage: exposes the plan for human review and allows early abort. Key failure mode: the plan can be wrong and the agent may rigidly follow it even when observations contradict it (plan fixation).
concepts.notes: Connects to Module 4 lesson 4.4 (Sherpa planning). "Plan fixation" is the named failure mode to watch for.

concepts.name: CodeAct Paradigm
concepts.definition: An agent paradigm where the LLM expresses its actions as executable code (typically Python) rather than as structured tool-call JSON. The code is executed in a sandbox, and stdout/stderr is fed back as the observation. Wang et al. (2024). Key advantages: composability (a single code block can call multiple tools, apply logic, and process results), expressiveness (loops, conditionals, data transforms). Key failure modes: code execution errors are harder to recover from; security requires robust sandboxing.
concepts.notes: Connects to Module 7.3 (sandboxing). The most expressive paradigm but with highest security surface area.

concepts.name: Paradigm Comparison Matrix
concepts.definition: A structured comparison of ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, and CodeAct across dimensions: reasoning style, memory requirements, failure modes, best-fit tasks, and latency/cost profile. Used as a decision tool for selecting the right paradigm for a given use case. E.g., ReAct for interleaved tool use; Reflexion for trial-and-error tasks with feedback; Plan-and-Solve for long-horizon structured tasks; CodeAct for data manipulation tasks.
concepts.notes: Practical synthesis tool. Should include explicit failure modes per paradigm to help students avoid known pitfalls.

concepts.name: World Bible (Recurring Business Scenarios)
concepts.definition: Three fictional but realistic organizations used as running case studies throughout the course: (1) HSBC Mid-Office Reconciliation — banking, regulated, high-stakes; (2) Helix Research — biomedical startup, cite-faithfulness critical; (3) Acme E-commerce — (truncated in module text). These scenarios provide concrete grounding for abstract concepts and force students to reason about evaluation, compliance, latency, and cost in realistic contexts.
concepts.notes: Pedagogical scaffold; understanding these scenarios is required to get full value from business-scenario sections in later modules.

concepts.name: Perceive-Reason-Act Loop
concepts.definition: The fundamental cognitive cycle of any agent: (1) Perceive — receive inputs from the environment (sensor readings, API responses, user messages), (2) Reason — process inputs to form a plan or decision (LLM inference in modern agents), (3) Act — execute an action that changes the environment (tool call, response, file write). This loop repeats indefinitely or until a goal is reached. The loop is the atomic unit of agent behavior across all paradigms.
concepts.notes: Bridges classical AI (Russell-Norvig) to modern ReAct. Every paradigm in 1.4 is a specific instantiation of this loop.

concepts.name: Cite-Faithfulness
concepts.definition: The requirement that every factual claim made by an agent must trace to a specific, verifiable source (paper, document, page). Critical in high-stakes domains like biomedical research (Helix scenario) where hallucinated citations can derail expensive experiments. Distinguished from general accuracy: a claim can be true but still fail cite-faithfulness if its source is not explicitly traceable. Represents a hard constraint on agent output quality, not a soft preference.
concepts.notes: Introduced in the Helix scenario. Connects to Module 5 (RAG, agentic RAG) and Module 8 (evaluation). Motivates the distinction between retrieval grounding and generation.

concepts.name: Human-in-the-Loop (HITL)
concepts.definition: A design pattern where certain agent actions or decisions require explicit human approval before execution. In the HSBC scenario: no automated resolution of breaks without human sign-off. Represents a hard constraint at the system boundary, not merely a preference. HITL is a dial position — the agent can do investigation/recommendation (dial 3) while resolution remains human (dial 0). Reduces risk of compounding errors and maintains regulatory compliance.
concepts.notes: First introduced in HSBC scenario. Connects to Module 10 (safety/audit) and Module 11 (business cases). Important that HITL can be selectively applied to the highest-risk actions.

concepts.name: Paradigm Failure Modes
concepts.definition: Named failure modes for each major paradigm: ReAct — "rabbit hole" (agent loops on one tool repeatedly, never reaching terminal state); Reflexion — "self-serving critique" (agent convinces itself its wrong approach was fine); Plan-and-Solve — "plan fixation" (agent follows outdated plan despite contradicting observations); CodeAct — "execution error cascade" (one code error corrupts subsequent steps). Knowing failure modes allows engineers to add targeted mitigations (timeouts, step limits, plan re-evaluation triggers).
concepts.notes: Highly practical. Each failure mode maps to a specific mitigation pattern introduced in later modules (e.g., retry logic in 9.2, reflection in 4.3).

concepts.name: Agent vs Workflow vs Pipeline Decision Framework
concepts.definition: A five-question framework for determining whether to build an agent (high autonomy required), a workflow (orchestrated steps with conditional branching but fixed control flow), or a pipeline (deterministic sequence of steps) based on autonomy requirements, exception handling complexity, and cost tolerance.
concepts.notes: Critical anti-pattern: using agents when workflows suffice. Module objective 3. Emphasizes cost of agency; forward reference to Module 11 (business cases).

concepts.name: Symbolic Agents (1956-1990 Lineage)
concepts.definition: The historical era (Newell & Shaw, McCarthy) of agents built on explicit logical rules, planning algorithms (STRIPS, GraphPlan), and knowledge representation in closed domains; foundational but replaced by RL and later LLM approaches for open-world problems.
concepts.notes: Historical context; explains why classical planning is less relevant for LLM agents. Module objective 2.

concepts.name: RL Agents (1990-2017 Lineage)
concepts.definition: The historical era of agents built on reinforcement learning (Q-learning, policy gradients, actor-critic) that learn by trial-and-error in simulatable environments; influential for multi-step reasoning but limited by sample efficiency and environment simulability constraints.
concepts.notes: Explains concepts like MDPs, value functions, that resurface in reasoning. Forward references to Module 2 (MDP/POMDP). Module objective 2.

concepts.name: LLM Agents Era (2022+ Lineage)
concepts.definition: The current era of agents powered by large language models (Transformers) that leverage pre-trained reasoning and language understanding to operate in open-world problems without explicit training, using in-context learning and tool interfaces instead of learned policies.
concepts.notes: Modern paradigm; borrows MDP/POMDP concepts but applies them via prompting not learning. Module objective 2.

concepts.name: Reinforcement Learning Agents (1990-2017)
concepts.definition: Agent systems trained via interaction with environments, using reward signals to learn value functions and policies. Formalized via MDPs/POMDPs; enabled breakthrough achievements like game-playing (Go, Chess) but struggled with sparse rewards and real-world complexity.
concepts.notes: Bridges symbolic agents to modern LLM agents. Introduces MDP formalism (forward-referenced to Module 2) and reward-based learning. Most progress in game domains; poor on open-ended tasks.

concepts.name: LLM Agents (2022+)
concepts.definition: Agents that leverage pre-trained large language models as reasoning cores, circumventing reward training by using in-context learning, prompting, and tool use. Replace explicit policies with learned representations in transformers, enabling broad generalization across tasks.
concepts.notes: Modern paradigm; combines symbolic planning structure (from agents of 1950s-1990s) with RL intuitions (exploration, reward signals via prompting) and transformer generalization. Central to the entire course.

concepts.name: Workflow vs Agent Decision Framework
concepts.definition: A five-question decision heuristic for choosing between predefined workflows (fixed step sequences, no loops), pipelines (linear data transformation), and agents (adaptive, feedback-loop-driven architectures). Emphasizes cost of agentification and when NOT to use agents.
concepts.notes: Critical decision framework for practitioners. Prevents over-engineering simple problems. Mentions 'cost of agency' and vendor choices. Forward-referenced to Module 11 (business cases).

concepts.name: Paradigm Failure Modes
concepts.definition: Each major paradigm (ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, CodeAct) has characteristic failure modes: ReAct may loop endlessly; Reflexion may not learn from poor feedback; Plan-and-Solve may create brittle, non-adaptive plans; CodeAct may execute unsafe or inefficient code.
concepts.notes: Important for engineering resilience. Learning objective explicitly mentions recognizing and avoiding these modes. Supports decision-making on paradigm selection.

relationships.reason: The agency dial operationalizes the agent definition into a continuous spectrum, replacing the binary "is it an agent?" question with a measurable 0–4 scale.
ReAct is a specific instantiation of the modern LLM agent definition, implementing the reasoning-action loop concretely.
Reflexion extends ReAct by adding episodic memory for learning from failures, creating a stateful learning mechanism rather than stateless loops.
Plan-and-Solve is a variant of ReAct that adds hierarchical structure: explicit planning phase before action loops, improving decomposition.
CodeAct unifies reasoning and action into code representation instead of separate thought-action alternation, trading structure for expressiveness in tool composition.
The agency dial is the measurement used in the decision framework to determine where a system falls on the spectrum, guiding the agent-vs-workflow choice.
Cost-of-agency calculation is a key criterion in the decision framework for determining when autonomy is financially justified.
LLM agents inherit conceptual frameworks from RL agents (MDPs, multi-step reasoning) but substitute learned policies with in-context prompting and pre-trained knowledge.
RL agents extended symbolic agents by replacing fixed logical rules with learned policies trained on reward signals from experience.
The agency dial provides the operational measure by which agents are defined and distinguished from workflows. It operationalizes the abstract definition.
Modern LLM agents inherit the planning and reflection concepts from symbolic agents (1950s-1990s), but replace hand-coded logic with learned representations.
LLM agents leverage RL intuitions (MDPs, reward signals via prompting, exploration) while replacing explicit policy learning with in-context learning from large pre-trained models.
Plan-and-Solve commits to a plan upfront before execution, contrasting with ReAct's online, step-by-step reasoning. Plan-and-Solve often uses ReAct sub-loops for individual subgoals.
The decision framework uses the agency dial (and cost considerations) to guide practitioners on whether to invest in agent-level autonomy or stick with workflows.
Each paradigm's failure modes are characteristics of that implementation; ReAct's loop risks exemplify the general concept.
Reflexion's failure mode (poor learning from weak feedback) is tied to its core mechanic of learning from past attempts.
LLM agents are a modern specialization of the classical agent definition (Russell-Norvig), using transformers as the reasoning core instead of explicit rule systems or learned policies.

optimizations.current_state: The agent-vs-workflow-vs-pipeline decision framework is described as five questions but no worked example is given showing how HSBC reconciliation, Helix research, or Acme E-Commerce would apply these questions.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a worked example showing one of the three World Bible organizations applying the five-question framework, demonstrating the decision process and justifying why agent (or workflow) was chosen with concrete cost/autonomy numbers.
optimizations.rationale: Learners need to see the framework applied to concrete problems before they can apply it themselves. Especially important for a decision framework that aims to prevent the "use an agent when workflow suffices" anti-pattern (module objective 5).

optimizations.current_state: The lineage from symbolic agents to RL to LLM agents is described historically but the course doesn't explicitly explain which concepts from RL (like MDPs, exploration-exploitation, value functions) actually reappear in modern LLM reasoning.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a forward-reference note in lesson 1.2 pointing out that concepts like MDPs and partial observability (POMDPs) from RL agents are re-examined formally in Module 2, and that techniques like curiosity-driven exploration map onto information-theoretic agent strategies discussed later.
optimizations.rationale: Helps learners see continuity across the historical narrative and understand why Module 2 (math) is foundational, not optional. Bridges historical and formal frameworks.

optimizations.current_state: Four major paradigms are described (ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, CodeAct) with failure modes mentioned but learners have no exercise to match failure modes to paradigm choices or to select appropriate paradigms for novel problems.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a classification exercise: give 5-6 agent task descriptions (e.g., "agent must handle exceptions without replanning", "agent must learn from repeated mistakes", "agent must compose complex tool sequences") and ask learner to select the best paradigm(s) and justify using the failure modes.
optimizations.rationale: Paradigm selection is a critical skill but passive reading of paradigm descriptions is insufficient. Module objective 4 says 'recognize and use' but only recognition is taught.

optimizations.current_state: The agency dial (1.1) and the agent-vs-workflow decision framework (1.3) are conceptually related but the module doesn't explicitly show how to translate agency dial scores (0-4) into concrete cost/autonomy tradeoffs used in the decision framework.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a section at the end of 1.3 showing a table: Agency Dial level (0-4) → expected token costs → autonomy gains → typical cost-per-error. Make this concrete by referencing the World Bible (HSBC breaks, Helix citations).
optimizations.rationale: Learners need to see the connection between philosophical framework (agency dial) and practical decision-making (agent-vs-workflow) to internalize both. Helps with module objective 3.

optimizations.current_state: Lesson 1.2 (Brief History) assumes learners can follow narrative about symbolic agents (1956) → RL agents (1990) → LLM agents (2022) but foundational definitions like MDP aren't introduced until Module 2.
optimizations.suggestion: In lesson 1.2, when introducing RL agents, add a sidebar or footnote defining MDP at a very high level (state-action-reward) and explicitly defer the formal treatment to Module 2. This prevents two issues: confusion from undefined terms, and the perception that history is disconnected from math.
optimizations.rationale: Learners need basic vocabulary to follow the historical narrative. A 1-sentence definition of MDP unblocks comprehension without requiring Module 2 upfront. Also prevents skipping Module 1.2 as too vague.

optimizations.current_state: The five-question framework for agent vs workflow vs pipeline is mentioned with references to 'cost of agency' and vendor choices, but no worked example is provided showing the decision tree applied to a real scenario.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a worked example using one of the three World Bible organizations (HSBC, Helix, Acme) applying the five-question framework to decide whether an agent or workflow is appropriate. Show the cost/benefit tradeoff explicitly.
optimizations.rationale: The framework is a critical decision tool for practitioners. Without a concrete example, learners may not internalize how to apply it. Using World Bible organizations builds continuity and helps learners see agents in realistic context.

optimizations.current_state: Four major paradigms (ReAct, Reflexion, Plan-and-Solve, CodeAct) and their failure modes are defined, but no side-by-side comparison or worked examples showing how each paradigm would solve the same problem differently.
optimizations.suggestion: Create a comparison matrix or worked example (e.g., solving a multi-step research task using Helix scenario) where the same query is attempted with each paradigm, showing outputs, failure modes, and token costs. Include concrete code snippets or pseudo-code for each.
optimizations.rationale: Paradigm selection is a core design decision, but learners need to see how each behaves on real tasks to develop intuition. Worked examples aid transfer learning to new domains.

optimizations.current_state: The lesson traces symbolic agents (1956-1990), RL agents (1990-2017), and LLM agents (2022+), but the connection to MDPs/POMDPs (Module 2) is not explicitly mentioned, though it's crucial for understanding the RL era.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a forward reference in 1.2 noting that the RL agents era was formalized using Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), and that modern agents still inherit MDP thinking (state, action, reward). Provide a 1-2 sentence teaser on why this formalism matters (covered in Module 2).
optimizations.rationale: Learners encountering Module 2 will see MDPs introduced without understanding why they're relevant to agents. Explicit forward-reference helps them see the lineage and builds narrative cohesion.

optimizations.current_state: Agency dial is presented as a 0-4 scale with 'four properties,' but the module text provided does not explicitly define each level (0, 1, 2, 3, 4) or the four properties.
optimizations.suggestion: Explicitly define each level of the agency dial with concrete examples: Level 0 (pure LLM, no loops), Level 1 (single tool call), Level 2 (ReAct loop), Level 3 (reflection/planning), Level 4 (hierarchical multi-agent). Show World Bible examples at each level.
optimizations.rationale: The agency dial is central to the module's learning objectives, and learners need clear, actionable definitions to apply it. Ambiguity here cascades to the decision framework (1.3).

optimizations.current_state: Learning objective 5 says 'Avoid the most common mistake: using an agent when a workflow would do,' but no exercise or assessment is provided to test whether learners can make this distinction.
optimizations.suggestion: Add a quiz or problem set with 5-10 domain descriptions (e.g., 'daily ETL pipeline,' 'customer support triage,' 'research hypothesis generation'). Learners decide whether each should be a pipeline, workflow, or agent and justify using the five-question framework and agency dial.
optimizations.rationale: This learning objective is about developing judgment and avoiding costly mistakes. Without practice, learners may not internalize the decision criteria or may default to agents (over-engineering). Practice tests competency.
